items.originalTitle: Cenk Uygur goes all in on Ro Khanna for 2028
items.author: Will Steakin
items.title: Cenk Uygur goes all in on Ro Khanna for 2028
items.summary: Ro Khanna hasn't launched a 2028 bid yet, but he already has a pioneer of the populist left in his corner. Progressive firebrand Cenk Uygur is set to formally endorse the California Democrat on Thursday night during his annual appearance on nephew Hasan Piker's Twitch stream, a Thanksgiving Day debate-a-thon the pair call "Cenksgiving." Uygur told POLITICO he will pitch Khanna as the best populist progressive candidate. His Rebellion PAC will also debut its first 2028 ad promoting a Khanna candidacy Thursday night. "For me, it's a no-brainer," Uygur said in an interview, explaining why he’s backing Khanna. "Who else would you back, and why would any progressive or any populist back anyone else?" Along with his PAC getting behind Khanna, Uygur is also launching his own "Draft Ro" website to collect signatures and showcase other early high-profile endorsers, though he wouldn't say who just yet. The endorsement is one of the first of the 2028 cycle, and it comes before any major candidate has formally announced. Inside Washington, Khanna’s chances are viewed as quite slim. But for Uygur, that kind of underestimation is exactly part of the draw. "I love it," Uygur said of the skepticism. "I wouldn't have backed him if anyone in D.C. was behind him." "We're running against Washington," he added. "So if Washington doesn't like a candidate, perfect." Uygur is pairing his endorsement with a litmus test he’s trying to lay down for 2028 progressives: Candidates must call what Israel has done in Gaza a genocide and support ending U.S. funding for Israel. "It isn't actually about Israel," Uygur said. "It's about: Is this person going to represent us or not?" Khanna, he said, is "among the very, very few, and maybe the only candidate, that'll pass that test." He allowed for one other: "There's also AOC. If she runs, that's another person that could pass the test." But that's as far as the praise goes. His endorsement of Khanna comes as many other progressives are waiting to see whether Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.) jumps in. Uygur isn't one of them. Asked if her entry would change his calculus, he said: "Not 1%." "Sorry, but I don't think AOC means it," he said. "I don't think she would do any of the things that she says, and so I'm not going to back someone who is not going to deliver." "She's obsessed with the establishment, so she's going to run a soft, weak race," he added. "She wants to make Democratic leaders and mainstream media happy. Good luck with that strategy." Khanna has told POLITICO he plans to decide whether to run after the holidays and that whether Ocasio-Cortez gets in won't factor into his decision. Uygur's backing could give the potential 2028 candidate some credibility on the populist left, not to mention a boost from "The Young Turks," one of the longest-running and most popular progressive shows online, which Uygur launched in 2002. He also co-founded Justice Democrats in 2017 and ran a long-shot bid of his own for the 2024 Democratic presidential nomination. His Rebellion PAC sparked controversy during the 2026 midterms with an ad tying U.S. funding for Israel to higher grocery prices, which the campaign of then-Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed distanced itself from. Uygur, who was also a prominent backer of Vermont independent Sen. Bernie Sanders' presidential runs, has a blunt prediction for 2028: "I'm positive Ro Khanna is going to win."

items.originalTitle: Shoppers helped pay Trump’s tariffs. Now Target, Best Buy, and Kohl’s are booking $387 million in refunds
items.author: Bilin Lin
items.title: Shoppers helped pay Trump’s tariffs. Now Target, Best Buy, and Kohl’s are booking $387 million in refunds
items.summary: American consumers helped foot the bill for President Donald Trump’s tariffs as retailers passed higher import costs on through price increases. Now the refunds are flowing back, and they are showing up in retailers’ profits rather than in shoppers’ bank accounts. Best Buy and Kohl’s both reported better-than-expected quarterly results on Tuesday, after Target beat expectations last week. Together, the three retailers recognized $387 million in tariff refund benefits in their latest quarters. The money traces back to February, when the Supreme Court ruled that the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA) did not authorize the president to impose tariffs, invalidating a significant portion of Trump’s tariff regime. As of Nov. 5, U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) had certified approximately $128.4 billion in tariff refunds, including interest, and sent them to the Treasury Department for payment, according to a Nov. 10 filing with the U.S. Court of International Trade. Tariff refunds are boosting retailers’ profits Kohl’s reported third-quarter comparable sales growth of just 1.2%, yet its net income jumped to $254 million from $8 million a year earlier. Much of that came from one-time items: a $137 million tax benefit, a $61 million gain from the sale of two properties, and $45 million in tariff refund benefits, according to the company’s third-quarter earnings release . The department store chain has received approximately $190 million in tariff refunds this fiscal year. It now expects those refunds to add $1.03 to its full-year earnings per share, nearly a quarter of its raised forecast of $4.30 to $4.50. Best Buy reported comparable sales growth of 6.1%, its strongest in five years, in Jason Bonfig’s first earnings report as CEO . Net income more than doubled to $353 million from $140 million, according to the company’s earnings release . In May 2025, Best Buy’s then-CEO Corie Barry said the electronics retailer had already raised prices on some products to offset the costs of Trump’s tariffs. This quarter, the company recorded $41 million in tariff refund benefits, which helped lift profitability. Target has recognized approximately $1.3 billion in tariff refund benefits in the first nine months of its fiscal year, including $301 million in the third quarter alone. Its quarterly net income rose to $1.2 billion from $689 million, and tariff refunds accounted for $228 million of that after taxes, or nearly a fifth, according to Target’s third-quarter results . All three retailers are seeing sales rebound. But the refunds are boosting profits without requiring them to sell a single extra product. Shoppers paid a large share of the tariffs Best Buy was far from alone in passing higher import costs on to shoppers. An April analysis by Harvard Business School researchers , who tracked daily prices of nearly 360,000 products at five major U.S. retailers, estimated that consumers shouldered up to 43% of the tariff costs in the first seven months after the new tariffs were imposed. U.S. businesses absorbed the rest. Trump’s tariffs amounted to an average tax increase of $1,000 per U.S. household in 2025, according to estimates from the Tax Foundation . In February, Goldman Sachs economists estimated that tariffs had raised core PCE prices, the Federal Reserve’s preferred inflation gauge, by about 0.7% through January. The effect outlasted the ruling. Researchers at the Federal Reserve Bank of New York and Columbia University estimated that consumer goods prices were still about 2% higher in August than they would have been without the tariffs imposed since early 2025. Some Americans who paid customs charges directly on overseas purchases are receiving refunds through shipping companies including FedEx , UPS , and DHL . The federal refund system offers no such relief to shoppers who paid higher prices at their local stores. Lawmakers are pressing companies to give the money back Earlier this month, Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.) and fellow Democratic senators asked the Federal Trade Commission to investigate whether companies that raised prices in response to tariffs and then kept the refunds violated federal law. Warren’s office accused corporations of “pocketing tariff refunds after raising prices on consumers.” The senators cited responses from five major companies: Walmart , Nike , Apple , Target, and Energizer. None committed to directly reimbursing consumers who had paid higher prices because of the tariffs. Several major companies have either ruled out direct refunds to shoppers or remained silent on the issue, as Fortune previously reported . In August, Walmart said it was using its tariff refunds to lower prices, having received nearly all of the $2.9 billion it was owed. CBS News reported that the retailer cut prices on thousands of items in July. Target is doing the same. In August, Target CFO Jim Lee said the retailer would focus on lowering prices but made no commitment to directly refunding shoppers. The retailer said last week it had lowered prices on nearly 2,000 home, apparel, and accessories products during the third quarter, on top of more than 10,000 price reductions over the past year. But lowering prices for future purchases is different from compensating customers for past ones. A shopper who paid more for a television or a piece of furniture last year may have no reason to buy another one this holiday season, even if it is now cheaper. This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

items.originalTitle: Kevin O’Leary told Gen Z to invest 15% of each paycheck. One worker asked why investors get the profits
items.author: Emma Witman
items.title: Kevin O’Leary told Gen Z to invest 15% of each paycheck. One worker asked why investors get the profits
items.summary: Shark Tank investor Kevin O’Leary rehashed a familiar pitch for Americans who want to get rich: spend less, save 15% of every paycheck, and let the gains compound in the stock market. But when O’Leary faced down 20 Gen Z workers in a Jubilee Media-hosted debate, one participant challenged the traditional bargain between labor and capital. Why should employees spend their lives drawing wages while investors get rich off the surplus value they create? “Why should all the money we make doing our work, our labor, why should it go to people like you? We did the work,” the participant, a software engineer named Joe, said to O’Leary. The episode of Jubilee’s YouTube series “Surrounded,” titled “1 Millionaire Boss vs 20 Gen Z Workers,” posted Nov. 15 and put the multimillionaire investor face-to-face with younger workers questioning the rules of the modern economy. The 8-minute exchange over whether workers deserve a bigger piece of the profits they help generate became one of the flashpoints of the nearly two-hour debate. The argument lands as employee ownership gets a mainstream hearing. SpaceX’s June IPO was expected to make more than 4,400 current and former employees millionaires, welders among them . And Mark Cuban has proposed that companies choose between giving every employee stock and paying higher corporate taxes . From Starbucks dividends to Amazon stock grants Joe opened with a Starbucks hypothetical: Why shouldn’t some of the chain’s billions in profits go to the workers making and serving the coffee? O’Leary argued that would shortchange investors who supplied the capital. Joe wasn’t suggesting workers get all the profits, just a bigger share. He pointed to Starbucks’ dividend payments to shareholders as evidence that the company already distributes its profits. Starbucks, which reported $37.9 billion in revenue for the fiscal year that ended Sept. 27, recently raised its dividend. The debate then moved from coffee shops to one of the country’s biggest employers: Amazon, which this year unseated Walmart as No. 1 on the 2026 Fortune 500 . Joe argued that the company offers one of the starkest examples of how pay can split by role. A software engineer with the same ability to execute and work hard as a warehouse employee could potentially receive substantial restricted stock units, or RSUs, as part of their compensation. The warehouse worker, meanwhile, might receive no equity stake, despite long shifts doing physically arduous work. Why, Joe wanted to know, should one employee have a chance to build wealth through company stock while another is limited to a paycheck? O’Leary said the labor market ultimately shapes compensation. If Amazon couldn’t find enough people willing to work in its warehouses, he said, the company would have to increase compensation to attract them. He also questioned whether equity could realistically be distributed across every type of business. “You can’t do that in every business. You can’t give equity to a utility,” O’Leary said. Joe said equity wasn’t the only answer. Companies could also offer dividends or profit-sharing arrangements that give employees a direct financial stake in their success. He pointed to O’Leary’s fellow Shark Tank investor, Mark Cuban, who gave employees equity at companies he founded and has urged every CEO to do the same. If investors can benefit financially when a business grows or is sold, Joe argued, employees who helped create that value should have a chance to benefit, too. The two did find one patch of common ground: SpaceX, where rank-and-file employees became millionaires when the company’s shares took off. O’Leary said he was perfectly fine with that outcome. Joe’s point, however, was that such windfalls are the exception, not the norm. The economy, as structured, funnels the gains from workers’ labor upward while asking employees to build wealth out of whatever is left of their paychecks. What investors bring to the table O’Leary wasn’t particularly receptive to the idea that investors were simply getting rich off other people’s labor. “I worked pretty damn hard to get rich. Really hard,” he said. Joe said that while O’Leary may have worked hard to build his fortune, he questioned what investors contribute beyond their money. O’Leary explained that he looks for entrepreneurs with promising ideas and business plans, then puts his own capital behind them. When Joe asked what he brought to the table, O’Leary answered bluntly. “Money.” The 15% rule meets the rent The exchange eventually circled back to O’Leary’s familiar advice about personal financial discipline. Rather than waiting for companies to distribute profits, he suggested workers take 15% of their weekly earnings and invest it in the stock market. O’Leary has repeatedly offered this advice to younger Americans. The investor has argued that someone earning $68,000 a year could retire a millionaire by consistently investing 15% of their income over a career. But Joe questioned how realistic that prescription was for people already struggling to cover everyday expenses. Earlier in the episode, another participant, a security guard named Kieran, described working 80 hours a week only to spend 55% of his income on rent. O’Leary said people could cut unnecessary purchases from their budgets. Joe pushed back, joking that O’Leary wouldn’t find much to criticize in his own winnowed-down wardrobe. The exchange ended on an unexpected note of encouragement. Apparently impressed by the passion of Joe’s argument, O’Leary told him he’d make “good television” and invited him to come on Shark Tank. Joe declined. “I never will,” he said. “I don’t want to be an entrepreneur, bro. I just want to live.” For a generation staring down rent, gas prices and student loans, that may be the more radical ask. This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

items.originalTitle: What Democrats’ Sweeping Midterm Wins Could Mean for the Redistricting Battle
items.author: Chantelle Lee
items.title: What Democrats’ Sweeping Midterm Wins Could Mean for the Redistricting Battle
items.summary: Voting booths at a polling location inside Wayne Community College - Eastern Campus on the final day of early voting for the midterm election in Detroit, Michigan, on Nov. 1, 2026. —Emily Elconin—Bloomberg/Getty Images Republicans and Democrats in several states engaged in a bitter fight to redraw congressional maps in their parties’ favor leading up to this year’s midterms. But in the aftermath of the blue wave that swept across the country, that conflict may be dying down—at least for now. Typically, maps are redrawn after the results of the U.S. census are released each decade, in order to account for population and demographic changes. Last year, however, President Donald Trump urged members of his party to redistrict mid-cycle ahead of the 2026 election as the GOP vied to hold onto its narrow House majority. Several Republican-led states moved to do so in the ensuing months, while Democratic leaders in other states responded with their own redistricting efforts, with varying degrees of success. The sweeping Democratic victories in the midterms, though, could mark a shift in the redistricting battle, political experts tell TIME. Read More: Are Democrats’ Stunning Midterm Upsets in Deep-Red States a Blip—or Is Their Map Expanding? Costas Panagopoulos, a professor of political science at Northeastern University, says that Republicans may be more reluctant to push for redistricting mid-cycle going forward, given that their efforts failed to counteract the blue wave in this year’s election . In states like Texas , North Carolina, Ohio , Alabama, and Florida , Democratic candidates came out on top in multiple districts that had been redrawn to benefit Republicans—which political experts have largely attributed to the fact that, despite redistricting efforts, Republicans were still facing a challenging political climate at a time when Trump’s approval rating was at a historic low . “In recent years, Democrats have been reluctant to engage in mid-cycle redistricting. Republicans have been more willing to do that, and Democrats have followed suit in response in order to counteract some of the districts created by Republicans to advantage themselves,” Panagopoulos says. “But as 2026 showed us, those efforts often amount to very little and can even backfire, so I think both parties right now are cautious about any mid-cycle redistricting efforts, and 2026 suggests that even if districts are very heavily gerrymandered to advantage one party or the other, there are no guarantees that those parties will win,” he continues. Mark Jones, a professor of political science at Rice University, says that, for Republicans, “pretty much anything that they could have done, they already did.” And he says that even if there are states where additional redistricting could in theory help make maps even more favorable for Republicans, GOP lawmakers will now face a challenging time pushing such legislation through if their power in the state governments was reduced—for instance, in Texas, where Democrats gained control of the state House and the governorship . Meanwhile, the Democrats who were advocating for redistricting in recent months were doing so as “defensive measures,” says Alvin Tillery, the director of Northwestern University’s Center for the Study of Democratic Governance and a Democratic pollster and consultant. And Jones says that, with the party’s sizable victories in this year’s midterms, “the sense of urgency” to redistrict “is no longer there.” It’s possible, Jones says, that some “unfinished business” may continue — for instance, Virginians passed a redistricting ballot measure in April, but the state Supreme Court prevented the newly drawn maps from taking effect; Jones says that Democrats could try to take up that effort again. But generally speaking, “I don’t think we’re going to see the gerrymander armed race in 2027 that we saw in 2025,” Jones says. If some of those efforts do proceed, he says, “I think it’s going to be at the margins.” “The Democratic Party reluctantly engaged in mid-decade redistricting only after Donald Trump and Republicans drew first blood, and given the size of the victory and the lesser the sense of urgency and need to bolster the number of seats that are safely Democratic, I think we’re going to see Democrats try to return to the norms that have governed U.S. politics in the modern era,” Jones says. That doesn’t mean that partisan gerrymandering has come to an end, experts point out. The next redistricting cycle will take place after the 2030 census, and Panagopoulos says, “When it’s a redistricting cycle, both parties engage to the extent that they can in partisan gerrymandering.” And Democrats, he says, “will remain better positioned to engage in pro-Democratic redistricting in part because of the gains that they made in state legislatures and governorships across the country.” “I don’t think redistricting is high on any party’s agenda at the moment,” Panagopoulos says. But, he continues, “Things will clearly shift in the aftermath of the 2030 survey, and what will be more important is what the partisan makeup of states and state legislatures looks like at that time.”

items.originalTitle: Airbnb CEO Brian Chesky says staff call him a ‘control freak’—but that he learned it from Apple’s Steve Jobs
items.author: Orianna Rosa Royle
items.title: Airbnb CEO Brian Chesky says staff call him a ‘control freak’—but that he learned it from Apple’s Steve Jobs
items.summary: Airbnb’s billionaire CEO Brian Chesky recently admitted that some of his workers probably call him a “control freak.” But he says he’s in good company, as he picked up the habit from studying Apple’s Steve Jobs. “People called him a control freak. He probably was a control freak,” Chesky told Time . “He held people to extremely high standards. He spent a lot of time recruiting. He was in the details.” When asked whether Airbnb staff would say the same, Chesky responded: “I think some people do.” He also spends 3 hours a day recruiting and tells his hiring managers to leave if they don’t like his input. But he insists that doesn’t mean he’s micromanaging his workforce—and he even talked to the man who worked closest to Jobs to prove it. Jony Ive worked with Steve Jobs for nearly 15 years—and said he wasn’t a micromanager Apple’s former design chief, Jony Ive, worked alongside the late cofounder for nearly 15 years in designing iconic products like the iMac, iPod, iPhone, iPad, and Apple Watch. And so Chesky once point-blank asked Ive what it was like working for Jobs. “Johny said to me, ‘I never felt like Steve was micromanaging,” Chesky recalled, adding that Ive’s felt like they were just “constantly partnering” because Jobs wasn’t outright telling him what to do. He just wanted to be in on the details. They’d even have lunch together every day . “Constantly working back and forth,” Chesky added. And that’s where the Airbnb boss draws the line. He said “micromanagement, where you’re like telling people what to do” is a last resort—and probably an indicator of how well they’re going to do at his company. “If I’m telling somebody what to do, they’re probably not successful,” Chesky added. “So the best thing is we’re partnering. I’m asking questions. What if we did this? What if we did that? Now I’m not doing that with my chief accounting officer, I’m not doing that with a tax attorney. I’m doing that in areas where I think it can add value, like product, marketing, operations, things like that.” Chesky has defended this idea before , arguing that “micromanagement” isn’t about control; it’s about helping people think bigger and move faster. In a previous interview, Chesky explained that being in the details shouldn’t diminish anyone’s autonomy or make your reports feel like the boss is hovering over their shoulder or undermining them. Instead, it should make them feel like their manager is invested in them. “So here’s the question: If I’m in the details with somebody, am I making them better or am I disempowering them? And I hope that when people feel like I’m involved in projects, they feel like I’m helping them push to think bigger,” he told CNBC . How Chesky micromanages his 7,300 Airbnb employees With over 9 million active listings in over 150,000 cities in 220 countries and over 8,200 employees , Chesky also argues that getting into the weeds is necessary to get things done swiftly. “There’s a paradox where being in the details sounds like micromanagement; it sounds like it’s slowing teams down,” the 45-year-old entrepreneur continued in the CNBC interview. “But when you’re in the details, you can actually help make decisions faster.” Essentially, layers of approval, endless meetings, and hours of wasted worker time can be saved when someone with real sign-off power is in the room. “The number of people in organizations that [have] to get through managers and managers and managers to approve something, but then all these leaders have to agree to something, there’s a bunch of meetings—peers can’t make fast decisions,” Chesky added. “Only a leader can make a quick decision in a room. I bring everyone in the room, everyone makes a recommendation, and we can make a really, really fast decision. “I think that’s the key of a leader, to make decisions,” he said. This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

items.originalTitle: Trump Accuses His Own Government of Falsifying Economic Data
items.author: Miranda Jeyaretnam and Chad de Guzman
items.title: Trump Accuses His Own Government of Falsifying Economic Data
items.summary: President Donald Trump participates in a Thanksgiving call with U.S. service members from Palm Beach, Fla., Nov. 26, 2026. —Daniel Heuer—Getty Images President Donald Trump has accused his own government of deliberately falsifying economic data before the midterm elections in which Republicans saw sweeping losses . “I would like to wish a Happy Thanksgiving to even those who issued fake Economic Numbers, just prior to the Election, and corrected them yesterday, three weeks late,” Trump posted on Truth Social Thursday. “A RECORD SETTING ERROR, and one so grave that it should be immediately investigated.” His holiday post also made jabs at the “Radical Far Left,” immigrants, and “Reporters and Citizens” who have criticized his White House ballroom project . On Wednesday, the Commerce Department’s Bureau of Economic Analysis (BEA) revised its estimate of third-quarter annualised growth to 4.3%, up from the advance estimate of 3.4% published on Oct. 29. Annualized growth tracks how much the economy would grow over a year if it kept growing at that quarter’s pace. The updated figures, which were published according to a prescheduled calendar, reflect an increase from 2.2% in the second quarter. In another post on Thursday, Trump called the revision a “massive, and purposeful, error.” “Why wasn’t the correct number issued before the Election? I am asking for an immediate investigation of this situation,” he posted. He did not provide evidence of manipulation. TIME has reached out to the Commerce Department and BEA for comment. It’s not the first time that Trump has sought to undermine economic data that didn’t reflect his claims of economic prosperity. In the lead-up to the midterms , Trump frequently claimed the U.S. economy was experiencing a major boom , citing stock market highs and pointing to his tariffs as enriching the country. When the advance estimate was published in October, the White House called it “the strongest pace in a year” and evidence of “an economy that continues to outperform the so-called ‘experts.’” Voters, however, appeared to see things differently: 76% said economic conditions were “not so good” or “poor,” according to the AP Voter Poll , and two-thirds said they believed Trump’s policies had driven up inflation. Nine in 10 midterm voters said the cost of living was a major factor in their vote. Reports on Wednesday showed a mixed picture of the economy. The BEA raised its estimate of growth in consumer spending and private fixed investment combined, pointing to stronger economic growth in the third quarter. At the same time, a separate BEA report showed that the personal consumption expenditures price index, a key measure of inflation, rose 3.8% in October from a year earlier. New York Fed analysts also estimated last month that Trump’s tariffs had added 2.9 percentage points to year-over-year inflation for consumer goods by February. Without tariffs, the researchers said, goods prices would have fallen slightly. Trump’s history of selectively undermining economic data Even before he became President, Trump questioned the integrity of economic statistics. “It’s a false economy that we’re living in,” Trump, who was then the GOP frontrunner, told CBS’ Face the Nation in 2015 , before launching into a diatribe against the unemployment rate. On the campaign trail, he called the job numbers “phony” and a “joke.” In February 2016, he falsely stated the unemployment rate was as high as 35% and that he “heard” it even reached 42%, while official figures showed the figure hovered near 5%. Later that year , without evidence, he called the 5% unemployment rate “one of the biggest hoaxes in modern politics.” But after his first inauguration, Trump slightly changed his tune on economic figures. In March 2017 , then-Press Secretary Sean Spicer was asked about a released jobs report, to which he responded: “I talked to the President prior to this, and he said to quote him very clearly — ‘They may have been phony in the past, but it’s very real now.’” At a round table in July that year , Trump acknowledged having dismissed unemployment figures before, adding: “now I accept those numbers very proudly.” The President has also accused the U.S. press, without evidence, of manipulating some figures to deny his achievements. In 2019, Trump accused the press of revising a 3.1% economic growth figure downward to 2.9%, when reporters were citing figures from Trump’s own Commerce Department. In July 2022, while out of office and speaking in Arizona , Trump slammed a 40-year record-high inflation rate of 9.1% under the Joe Biden Administration, and he claimed, without substantiation, that the actual number was much higher. “Biden created the worst inflation in 47 years,” Trump said. In August 2024, the Biden Administration’s Bureau of Labor Statistics preliminarily revised down the benchmark payroll growth for the year ending in March by 818,000 jobs. Trump called it a “ massive scandal ,” arguing that it wasn’t a revision but “a total lie,” and accused the Biden Administration of “fraudulently manipulating job statistics to hide the true extent of the economic ruin that they’ve inflicted on America.” In August 2025, after Trump returned to the White House, he fired BLS commissioner Erika McEntarfer , a Biden appointee, for allegedly manipulating job figures to reflect poorly on his Administration. “Today’s Jobs Numbers were RIGGED to make the Republicans, and ME, look bad,” the President posted on Truth Social at the time. The White House also published what it said was a “lengthy history of inaccuracies and incompetence,” citing revisions. Trump’s own former BLS commissioner William Beach and other federal statistical experts have said claims of manipulation have no merit and undermine the credibility of economic statistics. How the numbers are calculated—and revised The BEA routinely revises its estimates of annualized growth and other economic data. The agency bases its advance estimate on two or three months of available source data and makes assumptions where data is still missing or preliminary. When new data or survey results become available, the agency revises its figures to be more accurate. Those updates happen on a prescheduled basis. The advance estimate typically comes out around a month after the quarter ends, the second estimate about two months after, and the third estimate around three months after. For the third quarter of 2026, the BEA released the advance estimate on Oct. 29 and the second estimate Nov. 25, with the third scheduled for Dec. 23. The White House budget office published the calendar for all three estimates in September 2025. While federal policy allows for schedule changes in certain circumstances, such as the 2025 government shutdown, in this case, contrary to Trump’s assertion that the second estimate was “three weeks late,” the estimates came out on time. Wednesday’s revision happened because revised software price and retail sales data pushed up estimates of software investment and goods spending, while new Census survey data lowered the estimate of health care spending, the agency said . The agency cited new and revised Energy Department data for consumer spending on gas as pushing up overall goods spending. The 0.9-percentage-point revision was bigger than the BEA’s historical average of 0.5 percentage points difference between a first and second estimate. There are broader pressures that can make early economic estimates less precise. A Nov. 17 report from the American Statistical Association (ASA) found that response rates declined from 2016 to 2025 in eight of the 10 surveys of businesses and prices it reviewed. Fewer responses can reduce precision and force agencies to rely more heavily on estimates for missing data. Falling participation can also lead to bias based on which households or businesses respond and which don’t. Brookings analysts suggested in April that people may be difficult to contact, reluctant to respond because they are busy, or concerned about keeping their data private. “A falling response rate does not automatically mean that a survey’s estimates are inaccurate. It increases the risk that estimates do not remain as accurate and representative as they have been in the past,” the ASA said. The BEA has also faced staffing cuts under the Trump Administration. Its workforce shrank by around 21% from 473 employees at the end of fiscal 2024 to 374 by July 2026, according to federal personnel data compiled by the ASA . The ASA also found that the BEA’s fiscal 2026 budget fell around 8% from the previous year after adjusting for inflation. The association warned that staffing losses and funding constraints threaten the timeliness, quality, and availability of federal statistics. The agency, however, did not name these pressures in its explanation for Wednesday’s revision. Without responding to Trump’s allegation of purposeful error, Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick praised the BEA’s revised estimate as evidence that “The American Economy under The Trump Administration is doing BETTER than every expert estimated!” “This Thanksgiving, I am thankful to be a part of President Trump's administration, not only for the extraordinary honor of serving the American people, but because I love this Country so much, I know how much better off we are today than we were two years ago, and I know the incredible heights we can reach in the years ahead,” Lutnick posted on X. “4.3% Growth—Happy Thanksgiving!!”

items.originalTitle: Volvo's big batteries: We drive its updated 2028 plug-in hybrids
items.author: Jonathan M. Gitlin
items.title: Volvo's big batteries: We drive its updated 2028 plug-in hybrids
items.summary: Volvo provided flights from Washington, DC, to Copenhagen, Denmark, and accommodation so Ars could drive the XC60 and XC90 plug-in hybrids. Ars does not accept paid editorial content. COPENHAGEN, Denmark—If we lived in the world that Volvo’s product planners expected back when the current XC90 debuted in 2015 , both it and the smaller but related XC60 (which arrived in 2017) might have been the last of their kind as everything went electric . As we know, the future hasn’t turned out quite like that, especially in the critically important US market . At the same time, Europe and China are electrifying, which seems like an argument against spending resources on developing all-new replacements for models that might not have an eight-year lifespan in most markets. So instead, Volvo has given the XC60 and XC90 another lifecycle refresh. The exterior styling tweaks are minimal; the bigger three-row XC90 had already been given a new look last year, and the XC60 now gains a similar grille and the same matrix headlights, for instance. And that’s no bad thing—both were, and remain, handsome shapes that are popular with Volvo’s customer base. Instead, the Swedish automaker’s attention has been on bringing the technology up to date for model year 2028 standards. Which means a much bigger battery for the PHEVs, with sufficient capacity for a couple of days of daily driving for most of us before needing to be recharged. There’s also new, modern infotainment and interiors that are now even nicer to spend time in than before. Read full article Comments

items.originalTitle: The pig in the python in the marital bed: How boomers deformed the Silent Generation’s marriages, Gen X’s childhood and millennials’ housing
items.author: Nick Lichtenberg
items.title: The pig in the python in the marital bed: How boomers deformed the Silent Generation’s marriages, Gen X’s childhood and millennials’ housing
items.summary: The baby boom has been called “the pig in the python” since at least 1974, when Russell Baker gave the 76 million-strong bulge its name by using the disturbing image of a python swallowing a pig and struggling to digest it, just the way the economy is struggling to digest the bulge of the largest generation in history. It’s becoming increasingly clear, as the baby boomers push the median age of the U.S. population toward 40, that the generation is so big that it has created its own markets as it moves through life. In the current economy, this market-making dynamic is most visible in housing , where empty-nest boomers own 28% of U.S. homes with three or more bedrooms, compared with 16% for millennial parents, according to a Redfin analysis of Census data. The first-time homebuyer age has jumped to match the record-high median age of 40, the National Association of Realtors found last November. A new peer-reviewed paper suggests the python bulge was being felt decades ago in the marriage market of the 1970s and the bonanza in divorces that resulted. In an article titled “ The baby boom and the US divorce boom ,” published this month in the European Economic Review , Tereza Ranošová, an economist at the Deutsche Bundesbank Research Center, argues that the two postwar booms, in births after 1945 and in divorces about 25 years later, are linked. The U.S. divorce rate more than doubled between 1960 and 1980. Ranošová’s explanation is mostly arithmetic. “As men typically match with younger women, a large young cohort presents a supply shock to the remarriage options of husbands in existing partnerships,” she writes in the paper. So when the boom’s huge cohorts reached marrying age, the men just ahead of them, mostly the Silent Generation, born just before and during World War II, faced an unusually large supply of younger women. Those young women, meanwhile, were short of single men their own age, “making it more worthwhile for young women to match with already married men,” she writes. While standard models assume singles only marry singles, Ranošová treats married men as still on the market: “When younger women are abundant, some divorce to rematch with them.” “These men had the most options among women somewhat younger than them (who in turn were desperate for options, so they settled for already married men),” Ranošová told Fortune in an email. The paper finds evidence that some of those marriages ended in divorce and remarriage. She’s careful about how much this explains. “I would not want to overstate here,” she said. “I would say likely about a third at most.” She sees the boom as a push that “brought people closer to the decision,” while shifting social norms made divorce possible. “Once the norm was broken, it would be hard to attribute things to specific causes.” A market, not a morality tale The paper’s evidence is a comparison across states. Using 1960 and 1980 Census data on more than 2.2 million people ages 35 to 44, Ranošová found that people born in states with a bigger early baby boom were more likely to have ever divorced. The link held when Ranošová used World War II mobilization rates, which earlier research ties to the size of each state’s boom, to make it less likely that those states simply had different family values. The U.S. divorce rate (dashed line, by year) and the share of men who ever divorced (red dots, by birth cohort) rose and fell together, both peaking around 1980. Tereza Ranošová, European Economic Review (CC BY 4.0) The squeeze cut both ways. Early boomer women found men a few years older scarce, Ranošová said. Some married men their own age; others married older men, more often ones who had been married before. The paper also raises, without settling, the possibility that no-fault divorce laws loosened in the 1970s partly because demand for divorce was already building. Betsy Cox isn’t just a boomer — and a divorcee — herself, she founded Blackbook, which led the way in creating the “ divorce concierge ” service for the ultrawealthy. She hadn’t read Ranošová’s research, or even thought of the angle, but said “I totally agree with that” when asked by Fortune . “It’s very true, very true,” she said, adding that the boomers were “probably one of the reasons I started Blackbook Divorce. She recalled being one of the first people in her cohort to get divorced and then she saw firsthand the boomer divorce effect take flight. “I was the first, but then it was, boom! It was like, oh my God, crazy. It was everybody.” Cox’s business has evolved away from a pure divorce concierge; she’s just launched Blackbook Circle, which she described as a “private service that gives successful men a straight answer from a woman who’s seen it all, and then a team that handles it.” A lot of her new business consists of what she calls “AI guys,” who she sees as “refreshing.” “They’re not full of themselves and I think they would make good husbands and boyfriends because they’re nice guys,” Cox said. At the same time, she “100%” sees a divorce wave coming in as the AI wealth transforms lives overnight. Many of them want the traditional trappings of wealth. “They move maybe from San Fran to New York, a few of them. They want to be in the Hamptons, and they want to be into the clubs,” she said. The boomers are making the reverse commute, Cox said. “Those baby boomers that are in New York are now leaving because there’s a lot of men and women that, first of all, they’re getting taxed heavily — if you say New York or LA, but there’s nothing left.” She added that coastal boomers “feel like they’ve done it all. They have enough money. They don’t have to worry. They just can’t find anybody, and that’s a whole other story of how it’s not pretty out there.” The boomer wave had a long tail, when you look at the marital outcomes of Gen X and millennials. Gen X, children of divorce Gen X icon Kurt Cobain rejected the label of being a spokesman for his generation with trademark irony, writing the lyric “that legendary divorce is such a bore.” Nevertheless, nearly every alternative rocker came from what was called a “broken home” in the 1970s, from Billy Corgan to Eddie Vedder to Dave Grohl. The great music podcaster Yasi Salek, of Bandsplain, has argued that Cobain’s grunge genre was the product of a whole generation of American men reeling from their parents’ divorces. The numbers behind them are broad. In 1960, 73% of American children lived with two parents in their first marriage. By 1980 it was 61%, according to Pew Research Center . Before 1950, fewer than 2% of children lived with a single parent who was divorced, separated or never married. By 2000, nearly 25% did, the Census Bureau reported . Still, the famous claim that half of all marriages end in divorce comes closest to true for the Gen X childhood decade. Economists Betsey Stevenson and Justin Wolfers found that 48% of marriages formed in the 1970s had dissolved within 25 years. That’s the decade the baby boom hit the marriage market and Gen X was growing up. The divorce rate peaked around 1980, and each marriage cohort since has done better. By 2024, the refined divorce rate was down to 14.2 per 1,000 married women, according to Bowling Green State University’s National Center for Family & Marriage Research . Ranošová ties much of the decline to people marrying less and later, which she said means “better matches in the first place.” What stuck from the 1970s was the norm. Divorce went from rare to ordinary and never went back. Andrew Cherlin, a Johns Hopkins sociologist who has studied divorce for decades, wrote in 2000 that the American divorce rate doubled in the 1960s and ’70s, with a million children a year going through a parental divorce. Ranošová was reluctant to tie her mechanism to Gen X’s own attitudes toward marriage. “I think that would be way too much extrapolation. I have no evidence on that,” she said. The long tail The generations at the center of the boom kept divorcing. Among Americans 50 and older, the divorce rate doubled from 5 per 1,000 married people in 1990 to 10 in 2015, Pew found . For those 65 and older, it roughly tripled. Remarriages are a big part of it. Over-50s in a second or later marriage divorced at twice the rate of those married once, and 48% of the over-50s who divorced in 2015 were in a remarriage. Ranošová called it “not implausible” that her cohorts show up in those numbers. Those born between 1935 and 1945 being more often divorced in later life than the generation before “matches the mechanism,” she said. That could reflect both the original mismatch and the fact that more of them are in higher-order marriages, which “are statistically more prone to divorce.” Still, she guessed much of it “has to do also with less social stigma and a different economic role marriage plays.” The money stakes are real: retirement accounts get split and the lower earner can lose Social Security income, Fortune has reported . The divorce boom’s longest legacy may be fewer marriages. That matters for more than the wedding industry. University of Chicago economist Sam Peltzman has spent years combing the General Social Survey, which has asked Americans since 1972 whether they’re happy. His measure, the share saying “very happy” minus the share saying “not very happy,” ran at roughly +20 points on average from 1972 through 2018, steady through wars and recessions. Then 2020 knocked it down 22.2 points, by far the largest single move in the survey’s history, and for the first time more Americans said they were not very happy than very happy. By 2024 it had come back only to around +6, he told Fortune in May . Peltzman called it a “regime change” and something of a happiness recession. The crash split the country along marriage lines. Married Americans have scored roughly 31 points higher on his scale than unmarried ones for 50 years, a “marital premium” that held across gender, race, age, income and education. After 2020, the married fell, too, but stayed comfortably positive. The unmarried, about 45% of adults 25 and older, went from near break-even to -15. “We have a segregated happiness society,” Peltzman told Fortune . “I can’t see that persisting without consequences.” The zeitgeist found its way recently onto Saturday Night Live . On the Nov. 14 episode, host John Mulaney played a hippie at Woodstock in 1969, laying out his generation’s plans for later life. “Hey, when we get older, I think we should buy all the houses,” he says, and then floats skipping the dying part altogether. His fellow boomers didn’t seem to understand what lay ahead in their future. Later in the show came “Sister,” a fake ad for a service in which grown brothers hand over caregiving duties for their aging fathers to their sisters, who quit their jobs and move across the country to do it. Neither sketch is about demographics, but both run on it. A generation of 76 million set the terms of every market it entered: marriage in the 1970s, then housing, and now care, as the bulge reaches the years when it needs looking after — the pig is slowly exiting the python. items.originalTitle: Black and Latino workers are about 20% likelier than White workers to need a new career by 2035 as AI reshapes work, McKinsey says
items.author: Catherina Gioino
items.title: Black and Latino workers are about 20% likelier than White workers to need a new career by 2035 as AI reshapes work, McKinsey says
items.summary: Black and Latino workers are about 20% more likely than White workers to need to move into an entirely new occupation by 2035 as AI and automation reshape work, according to projections in a new report from the McKinsey Institute for Economic Mobility released Nov. 20. AI and automation could take over about the same share of work across racial groups, McKinsey projects. What differs is whether that work disappears. McKinsey estimates that automation could reduce an average of 21% of current U.S. work hours by 2035. Of the hours it takes over, 40% of those worked by Black workers and 41% of those worked by Latino workers would be displaced, compared with 37% for White workers and 36% for Asian workers, meaning employers would need fewer people, rather than an augmented environment in which the technology supports a person doing the job. The report ties the gap to the kinds of jobs people hold. Automation is most likely to replace tasks that are standardized, easy to check and low-stakes when wrong. McKinsey’s example is answering a routine billing question, as opposed to adjusting a patient’s medication dose. Tasks like the billing question make up a larger share of the hours Black and Latino workers put in. Physical work, which is increasingly exposed to robotics, accounts for 35% of Black workers’ hours and 39% of Latino workers’ hours, compared with 26% for White workers. The jobs most exposed to AI are predominantly held by Black and Latino workers. McKinsey Report “Our research indicates that while AI and automation are expected to affect a similar share of work hours across racial groups, the consequences may differ significantly,” Duwain Pinder, a partner at McKinsey & Company, said to Fortune in a statement. “While displacement doesn’t vary significantly between cognitive and physical work, the central question is not only how much work AI and automation technologies can perform, but whose work it replaces and through which types of activities.” The effects are projected to concentrate in specific jobs: Black workers hold more than their share of the workforce in each of the six occupations with the steepest projected declines in labor demand. Latino workers hold 43% of hand packer and packager jobs, 2.3 times their share of the workforce. The differences carry into projected job growth. Based on today’s jobs, McKinsey projects total work hours for Latino workers will grow 1.4% between 2025 and 2035 and 2.1% for Black workers. For White workers, it projects 3.4%, and for Asian workers, 5.8%. The report builds on the McKinsey Global Institute’s “Workforce in motion” study , which found that automation could cut demand for about 36 million U.S. jobs by 2035 while growth elsewhere adds about 41 million. About 11 million workers may need to move into entirely different occupations. Lower-wage workers are 7.6 times as likely as higher-wage workers to be among them. Only about 14% of workers who may need to switch have a direct path into a growing job, meaning minimal retraining and no pay cut. Among workers earning less than $38,000 a year, about 10% do, compared with almost 40% of workers in the top wage bracket. Private AI investment reached nearly $345 billion globally in 2025, according to Stanford’s AI Index, which the report cites. McKinsey finds White workers are 30% to 50% more likely than Black and Latino workers to work in the areas where it expects that capital, and the jobs and wealth that come with it, to concentrate over the next two decades, including AI software, semiconductors, robotics and biotech. The report also points to strain on new workers more broadly. It cites Stanford’s tracking of young workers , which found that employment for 22- to 25-year-olds in some highly AI-exposed jobs is 19% lower than it would be had it kept pace with less-exposed jobs. McKinsey flags risks that could make the gaps worse. About one in six U.S. households has no internet connection, and Black adults are roughly 80% to 90% more likely than White adults to lack broadband. A Stanford study of 4 million job applications cited in the report found that 26% of Black applicants applied to jobs where an AI hiring tool discriminated against their group. The report also argues AI could help at key points in people’s lives. It cites an AI model built on data from Medicaid-enrolled women that flagged pregnancy risks a median of 55 days before standard clinical signs. Simulations projected up to a 31.8% drop in adverse outcomes. On schools, it notes the evidence is mixed and points to New York City’s one-year ban on student-facing AI for pre-K through eighth grade. This is not the first time McKinsey has warned that AI could deepen racial gaps. In 2023, it estimated that generative AI could widen the wealth gap between Black and White households by $43 billion a year by 2045. The new report calls on employers to train frontline workers in AI and hire on skills rather than degrees. It asks investors to require bias testing of AI tools broken out by race, income and geography. It also urges states to use federal broadband funds to reach communities that are still offline. This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

items.originalTitle: Black Friday will put AI shopping agents to the test. Consumers aren’t buying it yet
items.author: Phil Wahba
items.title: Black Friday will put AI shopping agents to the test. Consumers aren’t buying it yet
items.summary: Earlier this fall Visa instructed 22 different personal AI agents to purchase three everyday items—a TV, a laptop, and a hair appliance—to see how they’d do. It was not a resounding success. Only 57% of the 15 shopping trips each agent made led to a purchase that matched the shopper’s needs or even resulted in a suggestion of something suitable. Many agents misunderstood consumers’ preferences or didn’t know what questions to ask, such as, “Is this TV game-compatible?” leading to many wrong purchases. The biggest names in retail have spent the year wiring their stores and websites for AI assistants, betting shoppers will soon rely on bots for their buying. Walmart made a big show of supporting agentic commerce early this year when it announced a partnership with Google and its Gemini artificial intelligence assistant to make it easier for shoppers to discover and buy items from the world’s biggest retailer. Target consumers using ChatGPT can now tag the assistant and describe an occasion they are shopping for and get back product ideas they can buy in a single checkout. Home Depot in August expanded its AI-powered shopping assistant, Magic Apron, to all of its stores after an initial limited trial. And earlier this month, OpenAI unveiled its “Wallet” that connects with American Express , Visa and Mastercard to allow agents to pay and close out a transaction based on the limits a human customer sets. But the Visa simulation illustrates the progress agentic commerce has made and how far it still has to go. This Black Friday-to-Cyber Monday weekend gives AI shopping agents their biggest stage yet, but the holiday season won’t belong to them. Instead, the 2026 holiday shopping season will be more dress rehearsal than debut. With the National Retail Federation forecasting more than $1 trillion in total holiday sales, retailers will be watching whether shoppers rely on AI just for gift suggestions—or whether they let bots do the buying. Small numbers, big bets Agentic commerce is already showing promise for retailers who want to get ready for what they see as the technology’s inevitable rise. A report by consulting firm Kearney noted that Amazon’s AI shopping assistant supported $12 billion in incremental sales last year, or 2% of total business, and Walmart earlier in 2026 reported that users of its Sparky assistant spent 35% more per order than the average customer. Emarketer research found that in the first quarter of 2026, AI-referred traffic to U.S. retail sites rose 393% on a year-over-year basis from an admittedly small base . A Bain & Co. analysis this month of Similarweb data found that AI assistants account for less than 1% of retailers’ web traffic. Still, retail executives aren’t waiting for these teeny numbers to grow before they start placing bets. Target CEO Michael Fiddelke told Wall Street analysts last week that agentic shopping was still behind only a small amount of sales, but that “it’s important for us to be at the forefront of any changes to the consumer purchase funnel.” Meanwhile, last month, Kohl’s CEO Michael Bender said that agentic commerce was still small but drew shoppers who spent more than average, and crucially he said he saw big opportunities for “purchase confidence” to increase over time. “We have an opportunity to participate in a larger pie. And our only question is: Which are going to be the best tools to partner with and how do we make sure it doesn’t add more friction?” said Macy’s CEO Tony Spring at the Fortune Innovation Forum in Detroit earlier this month. Cool, you go first Consumers are more cautious than retail CEOs. They are still getting used to the technology and seeing what it is capable of, and, importantly, what they can count on it for. A Morning Consult poll for Visa last month found that 54% of adults had already used AI for at least one shopping task, up from 47% last year. But only 23% of U.S. consumers trust generative AI to handle payment transactions on their behalf. That finding harkens back to the hesitancy consumers first exhibited towards e-commerce and mobile commerce. That caution faded with experience and time and as mobile payment platforms proved they were reliable. Now most consumers don’t think twice about paying for things online. For now, consumers are most comfortable using AI for search, and that too poses an opportunity. “Generative AI, more than agentic commerce, will play a significant role in this year’s holiday shopping,” says Anna Marrs, group president for global Merchant & Network Services at American Express. “Consumers are using large language model tools to do a better job searching for what they want.” The limitations of retailers’ sites themselves offer an opening for AI, says Forrester Research principal analyst Emily Pfeiffer. “Retailers’ websites are terrible at comparison shopping and surfacing things you haven’t thought of before,” she said. That is especially crucial for things like gift ideas or areas where a customer is less knowledgeable. “We’re more open to suggestions,” Pfeiffer said. Crate & Barrel Holdings CEO Janet Hayes says her customers are most willing to engage with agentic commerce when they’re building wedding registries. “When it’s complex and hard and they’ve never done it, they want suggestions,” she said. “The more they ask in there, the more it informs how to write better copy and give better content.” The option to search with natural language (“a hard-shell suitcase that meets Delta Air Lines’ carry-on size requirements and costs between $100 and $200”), versus clunky key terms (“hardshell+suitcase+small”), is also an advantage of AI. “[That] will make a huge difference,” says Pfeiffer. Her research found that 20% of shoppers will flat out refuse to shop on a website that can’t handle natural language. Black Friday and the holiday season may also not be the right use case for agentic shopping. An American Express survey found that 52% of U.S. consumers are fine allowing an AI agent to purchase low-cost items like household essentials and groceries, but only 15% feel that way for big-ticket items, like electronics and appliances. And a poll this month by marketing platform provider Zeta found that only 9% of respondents would let AI purchase gifts without personally reviewing them first. Growing at the speed of trust Moving consumers’ AI use from searching and browsing to full-fledged buying requires giving them peace of mind. “Consumers need to know what’s going to happen if something goes wrong. They’re going to feel good if they know they’re going to be taken care of if an agent makes a mistake,” says Kearney partner Katherine Black, who leads the firm’s food, drug and mass market retail practice. (Walmart said in October that its returns policy applies even when an AI messes up. “Customers are in control,” Walmart wrote in a blog post .) Retailers are looking for reassurance too. They seem to love the added traffic to their sites from AI agents but also fear loss of control of the customer experience and of customer data, which supports marketing and loyalty programs. In September, Amazon blocked Meta’s Muse agent from shopping on Amazon. (Walmart is taking a different tack: last month it rolled out infrastructure to enable third-party agentic commerce by creating a profile for agents that links to a shopper’s Walmart account.) The major credit card issuers have all unveiled technology this year that allows verified AI shopping agents to make transactions with all the protections consumers are used to. Amex has announced that it plans to launch its Amex Agent Purchase Protection offer to protect eligible customers from charges when a registered AI agent makes a purchase inconsistent with the customer’s authenticated instructions. If the 2026 holiday season experiment with agentic shopping is a success, then next year’s may well prove to be the tipping point for the tech. “It’s really going to grow at the speed of trust,” says Marrs. This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

items.originalTitle: The Metaphor Zoo by Jeremy Butterfield review – how animals influence our language
items.author: Kathryn Hughes
items.title: The Metaphor Zoo by Jeremy Butterfield review – how animals influence our language
items.summary: A lexicographer reveals the surprising origins of common zoological turns of phrase, from fat cats to fur babies Anyone who has grown up in the country knows that cows come home. They do it at tea time, like clockwork, because an unmilked cow is an uncomfortable cow. So how did “till the cows come home” come to mean never? Stranger still, when the phrase first appears in a 1587 commentary on St Paul’s epistle to the Galatians, there is only one cow. By the time playwrights Beaumont and Fletcher take it up a few decades later, their characters are kissing and drinking till the cow – still single – comes home. What began as a promise of endless pleasure has become a sigh of futility. Jeremy Butterfield’s Metaphor Zoo is full of such linguistic metamorphoses. Butterfield is a lexicographer by trade, the man the OUP entrusted with revising Fowler’s Modern English Usage. His guiding text is Lakoff and Johnson’s Metaphors We Live By (1980), which argues that metaphors don’t just colour how we speak but structure our thinking. In this sprightly but well-grounded book (metaphor alert), Butterfield asks what mental patterns lie behind the hundreds of animal phrases in English. Then in Johnsonian fashion, he sets about tracing the original, dating each through the Oxford English Dictionary and watching as it goes walkabout.

items.author: Margaux Seigneur
items.title: Thousands of girls and women report bleeding and miscarriages after French police use of teargas
items.summary: Almost 10,000 women and girls who took part in nationwide protests in October give testimony about disrupted menstrual cycles For three years, Naïma Di Piero says she barely had a period. The 46-year-old charity worker, who suffers from endometriosis, takes the contraceptive pill to suppress her menstrual cycle. But two days after being exposed to police teargas during France’s nationwide protests on 17 October, she began bleeding heavily. French police fired about 22,000 teargas grenades at protesters on 17 October at the height of the protests – equivalent to two grenades every three seconds (over 10 hours of maintaining order).
